concepts.name: Atoms, sub-atomic particles and isotopes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The nuclear atom (small dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, electrons in shells, mostly empty space); relative charges and masses of the proton, neutron and electron and how mass and charge are distributed; proton (atomic) number and nucleon (mass) number; counting protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions; deflection of beams of protons, neutrons and electrons in an electric field (direction and relative size of deflection, explained by charge and mass); isotopes, the notation with nucleon number and proton number, why isotopes have the same chemical but different physical properties (mass, density); qualitative trends in atomic and ionic radius across a period and down a group. Orbitals and electron configurations are achem.atoms.orbitals-configurations; relative atomic mass from isotopic abundances is achem.stoich.relative-masses-mole.

concepts.name: Electron shells, sub-shells, orbitals and electron configurations
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Shells, sub-shells and orbitals; principal quantum number; s, p and d sub-shells (number of orbitals, maximum electrons); order of filling of sub-shells up to 4p (4s before 3d); full and shorthand configurations ([Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²) and electrons-in-boxes for atoms and ions from hydrogen to krypton, including chromium and copper and the loss of 4s electrons first from transition metal atoms; ground state; inter-electron repulsion and spin pairing; shapes of s and p orbitals; a free radical as a species with an unpaired electron. d-orbital shapes (3dxy, 3dz²) are achem.transition.general-properties; ionisation energies are achem.atoms.ionisation-energy.

concepts.name: Ionisation energies and electron configuration
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Definition of first ionisation energy and equations for first, second and successive ionisation energies (gaseous species, per mole); factors: nuclear charge, atomic or ionic radius, shielding by inner shells and sub-shells, spin-pair repulsion; trends across Period 2 and 3 (including the dips at Group 13 and Group 16) and down a group; successive ionisation energies and the big jumps; deducing the electron configuration and the group of an element from successive ionisation energy data (values from the data booklet). Electronegativity is achem.bonding.ionic-metallic; Period 3 trends in general are achem.periodicity.physical-properties.

concepts.name: Relative masses, the mole and the Avogadro constant
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The unified atomic mass unit (one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom); relative isotopic mass, relative atomic mass, relative molecular mass and relative formula mass; calculating relative atomic mass from isotopic abundances given as a table or as relative peak heights; the mole defined through the Avogadro constant (6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹); converting between mass, amount and number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons); molar mass in g mol⁻¹. Interpreting mass spectra of molecules (molecular ion, fragments, M+1, M+2) is achem.analysis.mass-spectrometry.

concepts.name: Formulae, equations, and empirical and molecular formulae
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Writing formulae of ionic compounds from ionic charges and oxidation numbers (Roman numerals), predicting ionic charge from the Periodic Table, the ions to recall (nitrate, carbonate, sulfate, hydroxide, ammonium, zinc, silver, hydrogencarbonate, phosphate); balanced full and ionic equations without spectator ions, with state symbols; empirical and molecular formulae defined and calculated from percentage composition, from masses and from combustion data (masses of CO₂ and H₂O); anhydrous, hydrated and water of crystallisation, finding x in a hydrated salt from mass loss on heating. Using oxidation numbers to balance redox equations is achem.electrochem.oxidation-numbers.

concepts.name: Reacting masses, gas volumes, percentage yield and purity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Mole calculations from equations: reacting masses; volumes of gases using the molar volume (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ at room conditions, 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ at s.t.p.) and gas volume ratios (including the burning of hydrocarbons and finding a formula from gas volumes); limiting and excess reagent; percentage yield; percentage purity of a sample (ZIMSEC detail, Form 6); deducing stoichiometric ratios from experimental results; significant figures in answers. Solution concentrations and titrations are achem.stoich.solutions-titrations; the ideal gas equation is achem.states.gases.

concepts.name: Solution concentrations and acid-base titration calculations
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Concentration in mol dm⁻³ and g dm⁻³; dilution; standard solutions; amount from volume and concentration; acid-base titration calculations (simple, from a diluted aliquot, back titrations), finding a relative formula mass, the basicity of an acid or water of crystallisation from titration results; deducing the stoichiometric ratio of a reaction from titration data; using concordant titres. Redox titrations (manganate(VII), dichromate(VI), iodine-thiosulfate) are achem.electrochem.redox-titrations; titration technique and uncertainties are achem.skills.quantitative-practical; pH curves are achem.acids.titration-curves-indicators.

concepts.name: Electronegativity, ionic bonding and metallic bonding
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Electronegativity defined (power of an atom to attract the electrons in a covalent bond to itself), the factors that control it and its trends across a period and down a group; using Pauling electronegativity differences to predict ionic or covalent bonding; ionic bonding as electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, with dot-and-cross diagrams of sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, calcium fluoride and aluminium oxide (ZIMSEC detail); metallic bonding as attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons and how it explains conductivity, malleability and high melting points. Covalent character in ionic compounds is not examined. Giant lattice structures are achem.states.lattice-structures.

concepts.name: Covalent and coordinate (dative) bonding, bond energy and bond length
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Covalent bonding as attraction between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons; dot-and-cross diagrams of H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂, HCl, CO₂, NH₃, CH₄, C₂H₆ and C₂H₄, and of species with an expanded octet (SO₂, PCl₅, SF₆) or an odd number of electrons; coordinate (dative covalent) bonding in the ammonium ion and Al₂Cl₆; bond energy (for a gaseous covalent bond) and bond length; using bond energies and bond lengths (and bond polarity, ZIMSEC wording) to compare the reactivity of covalent molecules (for example N≡N and C–X bonds). Orbital overlap and hybridisation are achem.bonding.orbitals-hybridisation; shapes are achem.bonding.shapes-vsepr; bond energies in enthalpy calculations are achem.energetics.hess-bond-energies.

concepts.name: Orbital overlap: sigma and pi bonds and hybridisation
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). σ bonds by direct (end-on) overlap and π bonds by sideways overlap of p orbitals; σ and π bonds in H₂, C₂H₆, C₂H₄, HCN and N₂ (and the O₂ and Cl₂ examples ZIMSEC lists); sp, sp² and sp³ hybrid orbitals and the shapes and bond angles they give in organic molecules (Cambridge 13.3: straight-chain, branched and cyclic molecules; planar ethene); restricted rotation about a π bond; benzene's delocalised π system is introduced here only in outline and taught in achem.hydrocarbons.benzene-structure.

concepts.name: Shapes of molecules and ions: VSEPR theory
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Valence shell electron pair repulsion: bonding pairs and lone pairs, lone pairs repelling more strongly; the shapes and bond angles of BF₃ (trigonal planar, 120°), CO₂ (linear, 180°), CH₄ (tetrahedral, 109.5°), NH₃ (pyramidal, 107°), H₂O (non-linear, 104.5°), SF₆ (octahedral, 90°) and PF₅ (trigonal bipyramidal, 120° and 90°); predicting shapes and angles of analogous molecules and ions (NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, SO₂, ClF₃-type cases kept simple); shape and molecular polarity in outline. Shapes of complex ions are achem.transition.complexes-ligands.

concepts.name: Intermolecular forces, bond polarity and hydrogen bonding
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Bond polarity from electronegativity differences and dipole moments of molecules (polar bonds in a symmetrical molecule cancel); van der Waals' forces as the generic term: instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London) forces and permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces; hydrogen bonding (N–H, O–H and H–F groups) as a special case; the anomalous properties of water (high melting and boiling points, surface tension, ice less dense than water); effect of intermolecular forces on boiling points (chain length, branching, polarity); intermolecular forces are weaker than ionic, covalent and metallic bonds; ZIMSEC suggested experiments (deflecting a jet of water with a charged rod).

concepts.name: The gaseous state: kinetic theory and the ideal gas equation
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Origin of gas pressure from molecular collisions with the container walls; the basic assumptions of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas (zero particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions, random motion); pV = nRT with SI units (Pa, m³, K; R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) and unit conversions (cm³, dm³, m³; kPa; °C to K); determining Mr of a gas or volatile liquid; when real gases deviate from ideal behaviour (high pressure, low temperature, strong intermolecular forces) and why (ZIMSEC detail: validity of the kinetic theory for real gases).

concepts.name: Liquids, solids and lattice structures
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Kinetic-molecular description of the liquid and solid states and the interconversion of states (ZIMSEC detail); lattice structures of crystalline solids: giant ionic (sodium chloride, magnesium oxide), simple molecular (iodine, buckminsterfullerene C₆₀, ice), giant molecular (silicon(IV) oxide, graphite, diamond, and silicon, ZIMSEC detail), giant metallic (copper), and hydrogen-bonded (ice); how structure and bonding explain melting and boiling points, electrical conductivity and solubility; deducing structure and bonding from given properties. Nanomaterials such as nanotubes and graphene are achem.nano.nanomaterials.

concepts.name: Enthalpy changes and calorimetry
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Exothermic and endothermic reactions and the sign of ΔH; reaction pathway (energy profile) diagrams with ΔH and activation energy; standard conditions (298 K, 101 kPa); standard enthalpy changes of reaction, formation, combustion and neutralisation (and the ZIMSEC list of hydration and solution, defined here only in outline); energy transfers from bond breaking and making; calculating enthalpy changes from experiments with q = mcΔT and ΔH = −mcΔT/n (combustion and solution calorimetry, neutralisation, displacement), heat losses and other errors; thermometric titrations and temperature-time graphs with extrapolation (ZIMSEC detail). Hess's law and bond energy calculations are achem.energetics.hess-bond-energies.

concepts.name: Hess's law and bond energy calculations
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Hess's law; constructing energy cycles and using them to find enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly (from enthalpies of formation, from enthalpies of combustion, from two measured reactions); calculating ΔH of reaction from bond energies (bond breaking endothermic, making exothermic), and why bond-energy answers differ from cycle answers (average values, non-gaseous states); exact and average bond energies. Born-Haber cycles are achem.energetics.born-haber.

concepts.name: Lattice energy and Born-Haber cycles
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Enthalpy change of atomisation; first and second electron affinity (definitions, factors, trends in Groups 16 and 17, why the second electron affinity is endothermic); lattice energy defined as the enthalpy change when one mole of solid is formed from gaseous ions; constructing Born-Haber cycles for ionic solids with +1 and +2 cations and −1 and −2 anions and calculating any missing term; how ionic charge and ionic radius (charge density, ZIMSEC wording) affect the magnitude of lattice energy. Enthalpies of solution and hydration are achem.energetics.solution-hydration.

concepts.name: Enthalpies of solution and hydration
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Enthalpy change of hydration and enthalpy change of solution defined; the energy cycle linking lattice energy, enthalpies of hydration and enthalpy of solution, and calculations with it; how ionic charge and radius (charge density) affect hydration enthalpy; whether a salt dissolves exothermically or endothermically; using the cycle to explain the solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates is applied in achem.group2.thermal-stability-solubility.

concepts.name: Entropy and Gibbs free energy
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Entropy as a measure of the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy; predicting and explaining the sign of ΔS for changes of state, dissolving, temperature changes and reactions that change the number of gaseous molecules; calculating ΔS⦵ from standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); the Gibbs equation ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − TΔS⦵ with unit care (kJ and J); feasibility from the sign of ΔG; the temperature at which a reaction becomes feasible and the effect of temperature on feasibility; limits (kinetic barriers, standard conditions). ΔG = −nFE is achem.electrochem.nernst-free-energy. ΔS = ΔSsurr + ΔSsys is not required.

concepts.name: Redox: oxidation numbers, oxidising and reducing agents
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Oxidation and reduction as electron transfer and as change in oxidation number; rules for oxidation numbers in elements, compounds and ions; Roman numerals in names; oxidising and reducing agents; disproportionation; writing ionic half-equations and combining them; balancing redox equations with oxidation-number changes. Electrode potentials are achem.electrochem.electrode-potentials.

concepts.name: Standard electrode potentials and cell potentials
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Standard electrode (reduction) potential and standard cell potential defined (298 K, 1 mol dm⁻³, 101 kPa); the standard hydrogen electrode; measuring E⦵ for a metal/metal-ion system, a non-metal/ion system and two ions of the same element (platinum electrode), with a salt bridge and high-resistance voltmeter; calculating E⦵cell; polarity of electrodes and direction of electron flow; predicting feasibility of reactions from E⦵ values and its limits (rate, non-standard conditions); the electrochemical (redox) series and the relative strength of oxidising and reducing agents (including the halogens, ZIMSEC); constructing redox equations from half-equations. The Nernst equation is achem.electrochem.nernst-free-energy; transition-metal redox chemistry is achem.electrochem.redox-titrations.

concepts.name: Electrode potentials and concentration: the Nernst equation and ΔG = −nFE
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Qualitative effect of changing the concentration of the aqueous ions on an electrode potential (Le Chatelier reasoning); the Nernst equation E = E⦵ + (0.059/z) log([oxidised]/[reduced]) for systems such as Cu²⁺/Cu and Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺, and its use to predict feasibility under non-standard conditions; ΔG⦵ = −nE⦵cellF and the link between a positive E⦵cell, a negative ΔG and feasibility. Cambridge A Level only.

concepts.name: Electrolysis: predicting the products
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Electrolysis of molten and aqueous electrolytes; predicting the products at each electrode from the state of the electrolyte, the position of the ions in the redox series (E⦵ values) and concentration (for example concentrated and dilute sodium chloride); inert and active electrodes; electrolysis of acidified water and of copper(II) sulfate with carbon and copper electrodes (ZIMSEC suggested experiments); half-equations at the anode and cathode. Industrial electrolysis is achem.electrochem.industrial-electrolysis; quantities are achem.electrochem.faraday.

concepts.name: Industrial electrolysis: aluminium, chlorine and the purification of copper and nickel
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 5). Extraction of aluminium from purified bauxite (alumina in molten cryolite, carbon electrodes, anode replacement, energy cost); production of chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide from brine (membrane cell; uses of the products); electrolytic purification of copper and of nickel (impure anode, pure cathode, anode sludge with precious metals); production of hydrogen and oxygen by electrolysis; electrode equations and environmental and economic considerations, with Zimbabwean context where accurate (copper and nickel refining in general terms). ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Quantitative electrolysis and the Faraday constant
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Q = It; the Faraday constant and F = Le; amounts of electrons, masses and gas volumes liberated during electrolysis (including charge on the ion from data); determining the Avogadro constant by an electrolytic method (copper electrodes, mass change, current and time); sources of error in the method.

concepts.name: Fuel cells
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). How a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell works (acidic and alkaline electrolytes): electrode reactions and overall reaction; deducing electrode reactions for other given fuel cells (for example methanol); comparing fuel cells with conventional cells and with combustion engines (efficiency, products, storage of hydrogen, cost, source of hydrogen). ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Redox titrations and transition-element redox chemistry
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Using E⦵ values to predict the feasibility of redox reactions involving transition elements and their ions, and how a change of ligand changes E⦵ (ZIMSEC detail); redox titration calculations: manganate(VII) with iron(II), ethanedioate (oxalate) and hydrogen peroxide in acid solution; dichromate(VI) with iron(II); copper(II) with iodide and the iodine-sodium thiosulfate titration with starch; self-indicating titrations; percentage of iron in a sample, percentage of copper in an alloy, formula of a salt; other redox systems given suitable data. Titration technique is achem.skills.quantitative-practical.

concepts.name: Reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Reversible reactions; dynamic equilibrium (equal forward and reverse rates, constant concentrations) and the need for a closed system; Le Chatelier's principle and its use to predict the effect of changes in concentration, pressure and temperature, and of a catalyst, on the position of equilibrium (with given ΔH); which changes alter the value of an equilibrium constant (temperature only); ZIMSEC suggested household and food examples where accurate. Kc and Kp are achem.equilibria.kc-kp; industrial processes are achem.equilibria.haber-contact.

concepts.name: Equilibrium constants Kc and Kp
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Writing Kc expressions in terms of equilibrium concentrations, and Kp expressions in terms of partial pressures (mole fraction, partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure); units of Kc and Kp; calculating Kc and Kp and the amounts present at equilibrium from initial amounts and one equilibrium amount (no quadratic equations); homogeneous systems including esterification; how K relates to position of equilibrium. The relationship between Kp and Kc is not required. Kstab is achem.transition.stability-constants; Ksp is achem.acids.solubility-product.

concepts.name: Industrial equilibria: the Haber and Contact processes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The Haber process (sources of nitrogen and hydrogen, iron catalyst, typical conditions about 200 atm and 400-450 °C as approximate values) and the Contact process (sulfur burning, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, about 1-2 atm and 400-450 °C, absorption of SO₃ in concentrated sulfuric acid to form oleum); explaining the chosen conditions as compromises between rate, yield, cost and safety using kinetics and Le Chatelier's principle; industrial importance of ammonia (fertilisers, nitric acid) and sulfuric acid (fertilisers, detergents, batteries, chemical industry); chemical properties of sulfur in outline (burning to sulfur dioxide, ZIMSEC detail); laboratory preparation of ammonia and of ammonium sulfate (ZIMSEC suggested activities). Heterogeneous catalysis by iron is achem.kinetics.catalysis.

concepts.name: Brønsted-Lowry acids and bases
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The common acids (hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric, ethanoic) and alkalis (sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonia); Brønsted-Lowry acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors; conjugate acid-base pairs and identifying them in reactions (Cambridge A Level part); strong and weak acids and bases as fully or partially dissociated; qualitative differences between strong and weak acids of equal concentration (pH, rate of reaction with magnesium, conductivity); neutralisation as H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O and the formation of salts; pH 7 neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 alkaline. pH calculations are achem.acids.ph-kw and achem.acids.weak-acids-bases.

concepts.name: pH, pOH and the ionic product of water
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). pH = −log[H⁺(aq)] and its inverse; the ionic product of water Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K and pKw; pOH (ZIMSEC detail) and pH + pOH = 14 at 298 K; calculating pH of strong monobasic and dibasic acids (assuming full dissociation), of strong alkalis and of mixtures after neutralisation (excess acid or alkali); effect of temperature on Kw and on neutral pH. Weak acids are achem.acids.weak-acids-bases.

concepts.name: Weak acids and bases: Ka, pKa, Kb and pKb
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). The acid dissociation constant Ka and pKa; calculating [H⁺] and pH of a weak acid from Ka and concentration (approximation that dissociation is small, stated), and Ka from pH; comparing acid strengths with Ka and pKa; base dissociation constant Kb and pKb and the relation Kw = Ka × Kb for a conjugate pair (ZIMSEC detail: Kb is not tested by Cambridge); percentage dissociation. Buffers are achem.acids.buffers; titration curves are achem.acids.titration-curves-indicators.

concepts.name: pH titration curves and choice of indicators
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Sketching and interpreting pH curves for strong acid-strong base, strong acid-weak base, weak acid-strong base and weak acid-weak base titrations (starting pH, vertical section, equivalence point, buffer region, half-equivalence point where pH = pKa for a weak acid, ZIMSEC detail); choosing a suitable indicator from its colour-change range (methyl orange, bromophenol blue, phenolphthalein, thymol blue, thymolphthalein); why no indicator suits a weak-weak titration; plotting titration curves from experimental data (ZIMSEC activity). Cambridge does not use pKa values for indicator choice at AS Level.

concepts.name: Buffer solutions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). A buffer solution defined; how acidic buffers (weak acid and its salt) and basic buffers (weak base and its salt) are made, including partial neutralisation; how a buffer resists change in pH, explained with equations for added H⁺ and OH⁻; calculating the pH of a buffer from Ka and the concentrations (or amounts) of acid and salt, and the composition needed for a given pH; buffer capacity in outline; uses: the hydrogencarbonate (HCO₃⁻) system in blood, and soil pH and other examples (ZIMSEC detail: blood and soil); pOH of a basic buffer (ZIMSEC detail).

concepts.name: Solubility product and the common ion effect
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Solubility product Ksp defined for a sparingly soluble salt; writing Ksp expressions and their units; calculating Ksp from solubility and solubility from Ksp (salts of formula AB, AB₂, A₂B); predicting whether a precipitate forms (ionic product compared with Ksp); the common ion effect explained and calculated (solubility in a solution of a common ion).

concepts.name: Steam distillation of immiscible liquids
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Why a mixture of two immiscible liquids boils below the boiling point of either (each exerts its own vapour pressure; the mixture boils when the sum equals atmospheric pressure); steam distillation of heat-sensitive, water-immiscible substances such as plant essential oils (for example from eucalyptus or citrus peel) and its applications in the food, perfume and pharmaceutical industries; outline apparatus and the mass ratio of the distillate in qualitative terms (no Raoult's law calculations). ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Partition coefficients and solvent extraction
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Partition (distribution) coefficient Kpc defined for a solute in the same molecular state in two immiscible solvents; calculating and using Kpc; solvent extraction and why several small extractions remove more solute than one large one (calculated); factors affecting the value of Kpc in terms of the polarity of the solute and the solvents; partition as the basis of paper and gas-liquid chromatography in outline.

concepts.name: Rates of reaction, collision theory and the Boltzmann distribution
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Rate of reaction defined and calculated from experimental data (gradient of a tangent to a concentration-time graph; 1/time for a clock reaction); experimental techniques for following a reaction (gas volume, mass loss, colorimetry, titration of quenched samples, conductivity, clock reactions); collision frequency, effective and non-effective collisions; effect of concentration, pressure, surface area and temperature explained by collision theory; activation energy defined; the Boltzmann distribution sketched and used to explain the effect of temperature and of a catalyst; a catalyst provides a different mechanism of lower activation energy; reaction pathway diagrams with and without a catalyst. Rate equations are achem.kinetics.rate-equations; types of catalysis are achem.kinetics.catalysis.

concepts.name: Rate equations, orders of reaction and half-life
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Rate equation rate = k[A]^m[B]^n with orders 0, 1 or 2; order with respect to a reactant and overall order; the rate constant and its units; deducing orders from initial-rates data, from concentration-time graphs (constant half-life for first order) and from rate-concentration graphs; calculating an initial rate, a rate constant (from initial rates, and from half-life with k = 0.693/t½) and using the half-life of a first-order reaction; effect of temperature on the rate constant (qualitative). Mechanisms and rate-determining steps are achem.kinetics.mechanisms-rds.

concepts.name: Reaction mechanisms and the rate-determining step
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Multi-step reactions, intermediates and the rate-determining step; deducing a rate equation from a given mechanism and slow step; suggesting a mechanism consistent with a rate equation and the overall equation (for example the hydrolysis of primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes, the iodination of propanone in acid, and reactions such as 2NO₂ + F₂); identifying an intermediate or a catalyst in a mechanism.

concepts.name: Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts distinguished; mode of action of a heterogeneous catalyst (adsorption, weakening of bonds, reaction, desorption) with iron in the Haber process and palladium, platinum and rhodium in catalytic converters (removal of oxides of nitrogen, carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons); catalyst poisoning; mode of action of a homogeneous catalyst used in one step and regenerated later, with atmospheric oxides of nitrogen in the oxidation of sulfur dioxide and Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ in the iodide-peroxodisulfate reaction (explained with E⦵ values); decomposition of hydrogen peroxide catalysed by manganese(IV) oxide (ZIMSEC suggested experiment); enzymes as biological catalysts in outline.

concepts.name: Periodicity of physical properties in Period 3
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Variation across Period 3 (sodium to argon) in atomic radius, ionic radius, first ionisation energy (ZIMSEC lists it here), melting point and electrical conductivity, described and explained in terms of nuclear charge, shielding, and the structure and bonding of the elements (giant metallic, giant covalent silicon, simple molecular P₄, S₈, Cl₂ and monatomic argon); sketching and interpreting trend graphs from data.

concepts.name: Reactions of the Period 3 elements and chemical periodicity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Reactions of sodium to sulfur with oxygen (Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, P₄O₁₀, SO₂) and of sodium to phosphorus with chlorine (NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃, SiCl₄, PCl₅), and of sodium and magnesium with water (cold water and steam), with equations and observations; the variation in the oxidation numbers of the oxides and chlorides explained by outer-shell electrons; predicting properties of an element in a given group and deducing the identity and position of unknown elements from data (Cambridge 9.3). Reactions of the oxides and chlorides with water are achem.periodicity.oxides-chlorides.

concepts.name: Period 3 oxides and chlorides: bonding, acid-base behaviour and reactions with water
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Reactions of Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂ and SO₃ with water and the pH of the solutions; acid-base behaviour of the oxides and of NaOH, Mg(OH)₂ and Al(OH)₃, including amphoteric aluminium oxide and hydroxide with acids and sodium hydroxide; reactions of NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃, SiCl₄ and PCl₅ with water and the pH of the solutions; explaining the trends by bonding and electronegativity (ionic to covalent); suggesting the bonding in an oxide or chloride from its properties.

concepts.name: Group 2: reactions of the elements and their compounds, and uses
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Trends in physical properties of magnesium to barium (radius, ionisation energy, melting point, from data); reactions of the elements with oxygen, water (and steam for magnesium) and dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids; reactions of the oxides, hydroxides and carbonates with water and dilute acids; thermal decomposition of the nitrates and carbonates described with equations and the trend in thermal stability stated; solubility trends of the hydroxides and sulfates stated; predictions for other Group 2 elements; uses of Group 2 compounds (magnesium oxide, calcium oxide and calcium hydroxide in agriculture, calcium carbonate, calcium sulfate, barium sulfate in X-ray imaging, magnesium hydroxide and magnesium trisilicate as antacids; ZIMSEC detail). Explanations of the trends are achem.group2.thermal-stability-solubility.

concepts.name: Group 2: explaining thermal stability and solubility trends
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Why thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates and nitrates increases down the group: charge density of the cation and polarisation of the large anion; why the solubility of the hydroxides increases and of the sulfates decreases down the group, and the variation in enthalpy change of solution, explained by the relative sizes of lattice energy and hydration enthalpies; using data on lattice and hydration enthalpies. Cambridge A Level only; ZIMSEC asks for explanations in Form 5.

concepts.name: Group IV elements: trends and uses of the elements and compounds
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 5). Carbon, silicon, germanium, tin and lead: change from non-metal to metal down the group; structure and bonding of the elements (diamond and graphite, silicon, metallic tin and lead) and the resulting trends in melting point and electrical conductivity (semiconductors); properties and uses of the elements and compounds: diamond and graphite, silicon in electronics, silica in glass and ceramics, lead in batteries, tin in alloys and dental amalgam (ZIMSEC's 'tooth filler', described with care and without health claims), tetrachloromethane as a former solvent and why its use is restricted. ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Group IV oxides and chlorides; relative stability of the +2 and +4 states
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 5). Bonding, acid-base character and thermal stability of the oxides in oxidation states +2 and +4 (CO and CO₂, SiO₂, SnO and SnO₂, PbO and PbO₂; amphoteric tin and lead oxides); bonding, tetrahedral shape and volatility of the tetrachlorides (CCl₄ to PbCl₄) and their reactions with water explained by available d orbitals and bond strength (CCl₄ unreactive, SiCl₄ hydrolysed); increasing stability of the +2 state down the group (PbO₂ as an oxidising agent, tin(II) as a reducing agent) using E⦵ values where given. ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: The halogens: physical properties and reactivity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Colours and physical states of chlorine, bromine and iodine and the trend in volatility explained by instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces; trend in bond strength of the halogen molecules (and the low F–F bond energy); relative reactivity as oxidising agents (displacement reactions, E⦵ values, ZIMSEC detail); reactions of the halogens with hydrogen and their relative vigour; relative thermal stabilities of the hydrogen halides explained by H–X bond energies; reactions of the halogens with sodium thiosulfate in outline (ZIMSEC suggested activity). Halide ions are achem.group17.halide-ions.

concepts.name: Reactions of the halide ions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Relative reducing power of chloride, bromide and iodide ions; reactions of halide ions with aqueous silver ions followed by dilute and concentrated aqueous ammonia (colours, solubilities; the diammine complex formula is not required); reactions of solid halides with concentrated sulfuric acid (HCl only from chloride; Br₂ and SO₂ from bromide; I₂, SO₂, S and H₂S from iodide) with balanced equations and changes in oxidation number, explained by reducing power.

concepts.name: Reactions and uses of chlorine and the halogens
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Reaction of chlorine with cold and with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide as disproportionation (chlorate(I) and chlorate(V)) interpreted by oxidation numbers; chlorine in water purification (HOCl and ClO⁻ as the species that kill bacteria) with equations; industrial importance and environmental significance of the halogens and their compounds: bleaches, PVC, halogenated hydrocarbons as solvents, refrigerants and aerosol propellants (ZIMSEC detail), fluoride in toothpaste in outline. CFCs and the ozone layer are achem.halogen.halogenoarenes-cfcs.

concepts.name: Nitrogen, ammonia and the ammonium ion
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The lack of reactivity of nitrogen (triple bond strength, non-polar molecule); the basicity of ammonia (Brønsted-Lowry); formation and structure of the ammonium ion (dative bond, tetrahedral) by an acid-base reaction; displacement of ammonia from ammonium salts by alkalis (and the test for ammonium ions); nitrogen fixation in outline. The Haber process is achem.equilibria.haber-contact.

concepts.name: Oxides of nitrogen and sulfur in the environment
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Natural and man-made sources of oxides of nitrogen (lightning, internal combustion engines) and their catalytic removal from car exhausts; formation of peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) and photochemical smog from oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons; acid rain from SO₂ and NO₂, including the catalytic role of NO and NO₂ in the oxidation of atmospheric sulfur dioxide (with equations); environmental consequences of nitrate fertilisers (eutrophication, ZIMSEC detail); use of sulfur dioxide as a food preservative (ZIMSEC detail). Flue-gas desulfurisation and power generation are achem.environment.air-pollution-energy.

concepts.name: Transition elements: definition and general properties
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). A transition element as a d-block element forming one or more stable ions with an incomplete d sub-shell (why scandium and zinc are excluded); electron configurations of titanium to copper and their ions; shapes of the 3dxy and 3dz² orbitals; the four characteristic properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis, complex formation, coloured compounds) and why they arise (similar energies of 3d and 4s; vacant accessible d orbitals); relatively invariant atomic radius, ionic radius and first ionisation energy across the series; contrast with calcium in melting point, density, radius, ionisation energy and conductivity (ZIMSEC detail); paramagnetism from unpaired d electrons (ZIMSEC detail). Complexes are achem.transition.complexes-ligands; colour is achem.transition.colour.

concepts.name: Complex ions, ligands and ligand exchange
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Ligand (lone pair forming a dative bond to a central metal atom or ion) and complex defined; monodentate (H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻), bidentate (1,2-diaminoethane, ethanedioate) and polydentate (EDTA⁴⁻) ligands; coordination number; geometry of linear, square planar, tetrahedral and octahedral complexes with bond angles; predicting the formula and charge of a complex; ligand exchange in copper(II) and cobalt(II) complexes with water, ammonia, hydroxide and chloride (equations and observations), including partial substitution [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺. Colour changes are explained in achem.transition.colour; Kstab in achem.transition.stability-constants.

concepts.name: Colour of transition element complexes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Degenerate and non-degenerate d orbitals; splitting of the d orbitals in octahedral (two higher, three lower) and tetrahedral (three higher, two lower) complexes; colour from absorption of visible light of the frequency corresponding to ΔE as an electron is promoted, and observation of the complementary colour; why Sc³⁺, Zn²⁺ and Cu⁺ compounds are colourless; effect of different ligands on ΔE and the colour (copper(II) and cobalt(II) with water, ammonia, hydroxide and chloride); colorimetry in outline.

concepts.name: Stereoisomerism in transition element complexes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Cis/trans (geometrical) isomerism in square planar complexes such as [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (cisplatin as an anticancer drug in outline) and in octahedral complexes such as [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ and [Ni(en)₂(H₂O)₂]²⁺; optical isomerism in octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands ([Ni(en)₃]²⁺, cis-[Ni(en)₂(H₂O)₂]²⁺); deducing the overall polarity of such complexes; describing the isomers in words and tables (no drawings available).

concepts.name: Stability constants of complexes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Kstab defined as the equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion from its constituent ions or molecules in a solvent; writing Kstab expressions (water not included) including stepwise and overall constants in outline; calculations with Kstab; explaining ligand exchange as competing equilibria and the order of stability from Kstab values (a large Kstab means a stable complex), including the chelate effect of EDTA in outline.

concepts.name: Vanadium and chromium and their compounds
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Vanadium: occurrence in outline, oxidation states +2 to +5 and the colours of their aqueous ions (violet, green, blue, yellow), reduction of vanadate(V) by zinc in acid, relative stability using E⦵ values, uses (vanadium steels, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst in the Contact process). Chromium: occurrence (chromite, mined on the Great Dyke in Zimbabwe), the +3 and +6 states, colours of Cr³⁺(aq), chromate(VI) and dichromate(VI), the pH-dependent chromate-dichromate interconversion as an equilibrium, dichromate(VI) as an oxidising agent (tests for alcohols and sulfur dioxide), chromium(III) hydroxide as amphoteric, uses of chromium (stainless steel, chrome plating) and the toxicity of chromium(VI). ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Manganese and its compounds
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Occurrence of manganese in outline; the +2, +4, +6 and +7 oxidation states and the colours of Mn²⁺(aq), MnO₂, manganate(VI) and manganate(VII); relative stability; redox reactions of MnO₂, MnO₄²⁻ and MnO₄⁻, including MnO₂ as a catalyst and an oxidising agent and the disproportionation of manganate(VI) in neutral or acid solution; manganate(VII) as an oxidising agent in acid and alkaline conditions; uses of manganese (steel, dry cells). ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Iron: extraction, ions, rusting and biochemical importance
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Occurrence of iron ores and the extraction of iron in a blast furnace (outline, with equations); iron(II) and iron(III): colours, relative stability, oxidation of iron(II) by air, effect of pH and of the cyanide ligand on the stability of the ions (E⦵ values); distinguishing Fe²⁺(aq) and Fe³⁺(aq) with hexacyanoferrate(III) and thiocyanate and with hydroxide ions; biochemical importance of iron in haemoglobin (oxygen transport; carbon monoxide binding) and cytochromes; rusting as an electrochemical process and its prevention (barrier, sacrificial, galvanising); uses of iron and steel. ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Cobalt and nickel and their compounds
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Cobalt: occurrence, the +2 and +3 oxidation states, effect of ligands and temperature on the stability and geometry of cobalt complexes ([Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ pink octahedral ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ blue tetrahedral, with temperature as an equilibrium; [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ oxidised in air to [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺), uses (alloys, anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride as a test for water, vitamin B₁₂). Nickel: occurrence as sulfide ores (Zimbabwe produces nickel, in general terms), production and purification in outline (roasting, smelting to a matte, electrolytic refining), uses in alloys (stainless steel, alnico magnets, coinage) and as a hydrogenation catalyst (making margarine). ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Copper and its compounds
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Occurrence of copper ores (sulfide ores such as chalcopyrite), extraction and electrolytic purification in outline; the +1 and +2 states: colours and stability, disproportionation of Cu⁺(aq) to Cu and Cu²⁺ and the stabilisation of copper(I) in insoluble compounds and complexes (CuI, [CuCl₂]⁻); reaction of Cu²⁺(aq) with I⁻(aq) and its use in analysis; uses of copper and its compounds: electrical wiring, brass, bronze and other alloys, Fehling's solution in the test for aldehydes, copper(II) sulfate as a fungicide. Redox titration calculations are achem.electrochem.redox-titrations. ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Platinum group metals
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). The platinum group metals (platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, iridium, osmium) and the elements that occur with them (nickel, copper, cobalt, chromium in the same ores); occurrence in layered igneous ores, including Zimbabwe's Great Dyke (in general terms, no production figures); outline of extraction (mining, concentration, smelting to a matte, separation and refining) and why it is energy-intensive; uses: catalytic converters, jewellery, electronics, the platinum electrode and anticancer drugs in outline; value addition and beneficiation as an economic issue presented neutrally. ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Organic formulae, functional groups and nomenclature
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Hydrocarbon, homologous series, functional group, saturated and unsaturated; general, structural, displayed and skeletal formulae (described in words and text formulae, since drawings are not available); systematic (IUPAC) naming of alkanes (to C₁₀ for ZIMSEC), alkenes, halogenoalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amines and nitriles up to six carbons (and cyclic and aromatic names in outline: the A Level naming of benzene derivatives such as 3-nitrobenzoic acid is in achem.hydrocarbons.benzene-structure); deducing molecular and empirical formulae from structural formulae; primary, secondary and tertiary classification in outline.

concepts.name: Types of organic reaction and mechanism terminology
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Homolytic and heterolytic fission; free radicals, nucleophiles and electrophiles with examples; addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation, oxidation and reduction, with [O] and [H] in equations; the mechanism types free-radical substitution, electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution and nucleophilic addition, and at A Level electrophilic substitution and addition-elimination; curly-arrow conventions described in words (an arrow starts at a lone pair or a bond and shows the movement of an electron pair); inductive effects of alkyl groups and carbocation stability in outline. Each mechanism is taught in its own lesson.

concepts.name: Structural isomerism and cis/trans isomerism
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Structural isomerism: chain, positional and functional group isomers; deducing all isomers of a given molecular formula; stereoisomerism: geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism in alkenes from restricted rotation about the π bond and the need for two different groups on each carbon of the double bond (E/Z acceptable, not required); recognising chiral centres in a structural formula (including cyclic compounds) as an introduction; isomers in hydrocarbons, halogen compounds, alcohols and carbonyl compounds (the forms ZIMSEC lists per topic). Optical activity and drugs are achem.organic.optical-isomerism-drugs.

concepts.name: Optical isomerism and chirality in drug synthesis
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Chiral centres and enantiomers (non-superimposable mirror images) described in words; identical physical and chemical properties except the rotation of plane-polarised light (in opposite directions) and possible different biological activity; optically active compounds and racemic mixtures; why reactions via planar intermediates (SN1, nucleophilic addition to carbonyls) give racemic mixtures; relevance to drug synthesis: different activity of enantiomers (general examples, no unsupported claims), separating racemic mixtures, chiral catalysts to make one isomer; molecules with more than one chiral centre recognised (no meso compounds or diastereoisomers).

concepts.name: Organic synthesis with AS Level reactions
concepts.description: Cambridge only (AS Level). Using the AS Level reactions (alkanes, alkenes, halogenoalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes and ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, nitriles and amines) to identify functional groups in a molecule with several groups and predict its reactions; devising two- and three-step synthetic routes (including adding a carbon atom via a nitrile); analysing a given route: type of reaction, reagents and conditions for each step, possible by-products; reaction maps given as tables. Cambridge AS Level (21.1).

concepts.name: Multi-step synthesis with A Level reactions
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Extending synthesis to the A Level reactions (arenes and Friedel-Crafts, halogenoarenes, phenol, acyl chlorides, amines, phenylamine and azo compounds, amides, amino acids, condensation polymers, LiAlH₄ reductions); multi-step routes for aromatic and aliphatic targets; analysing routes for reaction types, reagents, conditions, by-products and chirality of products; combining synthesis with spectroscopic identification in outline. Cambridge A Level only (36.1).

concepts.name: Alkanes, crude oil and combustion
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Crude oil and natural gas as sources of hydrocarbons; fractional distillation and the decrease in volatility (rise in boiling point) with chain length, and lower boiling points of branched isomers; cracking (heat with Al₂O₃ or another catalyst) to obtain more useful smaller alkanes and alkenes, with equations; production of alkanes by hydrogenation of alkenes; general unreactivity of alkanes (strong, non-polar C–H bonds); complete and incomplete combustion; environmental consequences of carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons from engines and their catalytic removal; demonstrating cracking with paraffin or cooking oil (ZIMSEC suggested activity). Free-radical substitution is achem.hydrocarbons.free-radical-substitution.

concepts.name: Free-radical substitution of alkanes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Reaction of alkanes such as ethane and methane with chlorine or bromine in ultraviolet light; the mechanism by homolytic fission: initiation, propagation and termination steps with equations (radicals shown with a dot); why a mixture of products forms (further substitution, termination products such as butane from ethane); predicting products and the number of monosubstituted isomers.

concepts.name: Alkenes: preparation and reactions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Production of alkenes by elimination of HX from halogenoalkanes (ethanolic NaOH, heat), dehydration of alcohols (heated Al₂O₃ or concentrated H₂SO₄/H₃PO₄) and cracking; addition reactions of ethene and propene: hydrogen (Ni or Pt, heat), steam (H₃PO₄ catalyst), hydrogen halides, halogens; oxidation by cold dilute acidified manganate(VII) to a diol and by hot concentrated acidified manganate(VII) with rupture of the C=C bond, and deducing the position of a double bond from the products; aqueous bromine as a test for C=C; addition polymerisation in outline (taught in achem.polymers.addition). The mechanism is achem.hydrocarbons.electrophilic-addition.

concepts.name: Electrophilic addition mechanism
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). The mechanism of electrophilic addition described step by step with curly arrows in words: bromine to ethene (induced dipole, carbocation, bromide attack; evidence from bromine water with other anions in outline) and hydrogen bromide to propene; inductive effect of alkyl groups and the stability of primary, secondary and tertiary carbocations; Markovnikov addition explained and the major and minor products predicted.

concepts.name: The structure of benzene and naming aromatic compounds
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Kekulé model and its problems (equal bond lengths, enthalpy of hydrogenation smaller than expected, resistance to addition); the delocalised model: sp² carbon atoms, σ framework, overlapping p orbitals forming a delocalised π system above and below a planar ring with 120° angles; aromatic stabilisation (delocalisation energy calculated from hydrogenation enthalpies); naming simple aromatic compounds with one benzene ring and substituents (for example methylbenzene, 2,4,6-tribromophenol, 3-nitrobenzoic acid) and the A Level formula conventions (Cambridge 29.1-29.3). ZIMSEC describes benzene bonding by orbital overlap. Reactions are achem.hydrocarbons.arenes-reactions.

concepts.name: Reactions of benzene and methylbenzene
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Reactions of benzene and methylbenzene: halogenation with Cl₂ or Br₂ and an AlCl₃/AlBr₃ (or iron) catalyst; nitration with concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids at 25-60 °C; Friedel-Crafts alkylation (CH₃Cl, AlCl₃) and acylation (CH₃COCl, AlCl₃); oxidation of the side chain to benzoic acid with hot alkaline manganate(VII) then acid; hydrogenation of the ring (H₂, Pt or Ni, heat) to cyclohexane; halogenation in the side chain (ultraviolet light, free radical) versus in the ring (halogen carrier) depending on conditions; directing effects of –NH₂, –OH, –R (2,4-directing) and –NO₂, –COOH, –COR (3-directing). The mechanism is achem.hydrocarbons.electrophilic-substitution.

concepts.name: Electrophilic substitution mechanism in arenes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Generating the electrophile (NO₂⁺ from the nitrating mixture; Br⁺ or a polarised Br–Br–AlBr₃ complex from the halogen carrier; carbocations or acylium ions in Friedel-Crafts reactions); the mechanism of nitration and bromination of benzene described step by step (attack by the π system, intermediate with the delocalisation partly disrupted, loss of H⁺ restoring the ring); why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition (aromatic stabilisation); comparison with electrophilic addition to alkenes.

concepts.name: Halogenoalkanes: preparation and reactions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Production of halogenoalkanes (free-radical substitution of alkanes, addition of HX or X₂ to alkenes, substitution of alcohols with HX, KCl/concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄, PCl₃, PCl₅ or SOCl₂); naming and classifying as primary, secondary and tertiary; isomerism in halogenoalkanes; nucleophilic substitution with NaOH(aq) to alcohols, KCN in ethanol to nitriles, NH₃ in ethanol under pressure to amines (as exemplified by bromoethane); elimination with NaOH in ethanol to alkenes (bromoethane, 2-bromopropane); identifying the halogen with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol; relative reactivity of chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes explained by C–X bond energy rather than polarity. Mechanisms are achem.halogen.sn1-sn2.

concepts.name: Nucleophilic substitution mechanisms: SN1 and SN2
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). SN2 mechanism (one step, transition state, inversion, rate = k[RX][OH⁻]) and SN1 mechanism (carbocation intermediate, rate-determining ionisation, rate = k[RX], racemisation) described step by step in words; primary halogenoalkanes react mainly by SN2, tertiary by SN1, secondary by both; inductive effect of alkyl groups and steric hindrance; competition between substitution and elimination (aqueous versus ethanolic conditions). Rate equations are linked to achem.kinetics.mechanisms-rds.

concepts.name: Halogenoarenes, fluoroalkanes and CFCs
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Production of halogenoarenes (chlorobenzene from benzene; 2- and 4-chloromethylbenzene from methylbenzene with Cl₂ and AlCl₃); why chlorobenzene is much less reactive than chloroethane towards hydrolysis (partial double-bond character of C–Cl from delocalisation of a chlorine lone pair, stronger bond, repulsion of nucleophiles by the π system); uses of fluoroalkanes and fluorohalogenoalkanes based on their chemical inertness (refrigerants, propellants, anaesthetics, non-stick coatings); the concern about chlorofluoroalkanes (CFCs) and the ozone layer (chlorine radicals from photodissociation, catalytic ozone destruction with equations) and replacement compounds.

concepts.name: Alcohols: structure, physical properties and the manufacture of ethanol
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Naming and classifying primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols (including diols and other molecules with more than one –OH); structural isomers of alcohols; physical properties (boiling points and solubility in water) explained by hydrogen bonding; manufacture of ethanol by fermentation of sugars with yeast (conditions, equation, distillation; Zimbabwean examples such as fruits of the marula or baobab, or sugar cane, in general terms) and by hydration of ethene (steam, H₃PO₄ catalyst), compared; acidity of alcohols compared with water (Cambridge 16.1.5). Reactions of alcohols are achem.hydroxy.alcohol-reactions.

concepts.name: Reactions of alcohols
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Production of alcohols (hydration of alkenes; cold dilute manganate(VII) on alkenes to diols; hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes; reduction of aldehydes and ketones with NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ and of carboxylic acids with LiAlH₄; hydrolysis of esters); combustion; substitution to halogenoalkanes; reaction with sodium; oxidation by acidified dichromate(VI) or manganate(VII): primary to aldehydes (distil) and carboxylic acids (reflux), secondary to ketones, tertiary not oxidised, with the orange-to-green colour change as a distinguishing test; dehydration to alkenes; esterification with carboxylic acids (concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst); the tri-iodomethane (iodoform) test with alkaline iodine for CH₃CH(OH)– alcohols, with the products. Esters from acyl chlorides are achem.carboxylic.acyl-chlorides.

concepts.name: Phenol
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Production of phenol from phenylamine via the diazonium salt (NaNO₂ and dilute acid below 10 °C, then warming in water); acidity of phenol explained by delocalisation of the negative charge in the phenoxide ion, and the relative acidities of water, phenol and ethanol; reactions with NaOH(aq) and with sodium to form sodium phenoxide; coupling with diazonium salts in alkali to form azo dyes; nitration with dilute nitric acid at room temperature (2- and 4-nitrophenol) and bromination with bromine water (2,4,6-tribromophenol, white precipitate) and why these conditions are milder than for benzene; –OH directs to the 2-, 4- and 6-positions; applying the reactions to other phenols such as naphthol.

concepts.name: Aldehydes and ketones: preparation, reduction and tests
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Naming aldehydes and ketones and their isomerism (including functional-group isomers of each other); preparation by oxidation of primary alcohols (distillation) and secondary alcohols; reduction with NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ to primary and secondary alcohols; tests: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (orange precipitate for any carbonyl), Fehling's or Benedict's solution (red-brown precipitate), Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and acidified dichromate(VI) to distinguish aldehydes from ketones; the tri-iodomethane test for CH₃CO– compounds, with the products; deducing the identity of an unknown carbonyl compound from test results and derivative melting points in outline. Nucleophilic addition is achem.carbonyl.nucleophilic-addition.

concepts.name: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyl compounds
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Polarity of the C=O bond; reaction of aldehydes and ketones (ethanal and propanone) with HCN with KCN as catalyst to form hydroxynitriles; the nucleophilic addition mechanism described step by step in words (cyanide attack on the δ+ carbon, alkoxide intermediate, protonation); why a racemic mixture can form; use of hydroxynitriles to lengthen the carbon chain (hydrolysis to hydroxy acids, reduction to amines in outline); reduction by hydride ions as nucleophilic addition in outline; relative reactivity of aldehydes and ketones.

concepts.name: Carboxylic acids: preparation and reactions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Naming carboxylic acids and their occurrence (ethanoic acid in vinegar, citric acid in citrus fruit, methanoic acid in ant stings); production by oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes (reflux), hydrolysis of nitriles and of esters followed by acidification; reactions as acids with reactive metals, alkalis and carbonates; esterification with alcohols (concentrated H₂SO₄); reduction by LiAlH₄ to primary alcohols. Relative acidity and the A Level reactions are achem.carboxylic.acidity-further-reactions.

concepts.name: Acidity of carboxylic acids; further reactions of acids
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Relative acidities of carboxylic acids, phenols, alcohols and water explained by the stability of the anion (delocalisation in the carboxylate ion); effect of chlorine substitution on the acidity of ethanoic acid (chloro-, dichloro-, trichloroethanoic acids, inductive effect; pKa data); production of benzoic acid by oxidising methylbenzene with hot alkaline manganate(VII); conversion of carboxylic acids to acyl chlorides with PCl₅, PCl₃ (heat) or SOCl₂; oxidation of methanoic acid (Fehling's, Tollens', acidified manganate(VII) or dichromate(VI)) and of ethanedioic acid (warm acidified manganate(VII)) to carbon dioxide.

concepts.name: Esters: formation, hydrolysis, soap and uses
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Naming esters (up to six plus six carbons); formation by condensation of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol with a concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst (ethyl ethanoate) and as an equilibrium; acid hydrolysis (reversible) and base hydrolysis (saponification, goes to completion) of esters; fats and oils as esters of propane-1,2,3-triol and making soap from fats or oils and alkali (ZIMSEC suggested activity with wood ash); uses of esters (flavourings, perfumes, solvents) and of carboxylic acids (food preservation, vinegar, making esters and polymers) (ZIMSEC detail). Esters from acyl chlorides and phenol (phenyl benzoate) are achem.carboxylic.acyl-chlorides.

concepts.name: Acyl chlorides and the addition-elimination mechanism
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Preparation of acyl chlorides from carboxylic acids (PCl₅, PCl₃ with heat, SOCl₂); reactions at room temperature with water (carboxylic acid and HCl), alcohols (esters, for example ethyl ethanoate), phenol (phenyl esters, for example phenyl benzoate, which cannot be made directly from the acid), ammonia (amides) and primary or secondary amines (substituted amides); the addition-elimination mechanism described step by step in words; relative ease of hydrolysis of acyl chlorides, alkyl chlorides and aryl chlorides explained by structure.

concepts.name: Amines: preparation and basicity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Primary, secondary and tertiary amines (naming of secondary and tertiary amines not required); production of primary and secondary amines: halogenoalkanes with excess ammonia or with a primary amine in ethanol under pressure, reduction of amides with LiAlH₄ and of nitriles with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni (ethylamine from ethanenitrile); basicity of aqueous amines and the relative basicities of ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine explained by the availability of the nitrogen lone pair (inductive effect of alkyl groups; delocalisation into the benzene ring); salt formation with acids; condensation with acyl chlorides to amides. Cambridge A Level (AS only examines amine formation from halogenoalkanes).

concepts.name: Nitriles and hydroxynitriles
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Naming nitriles (straight chains); production of nitriles from halogenoalkanes and KCN in ethanol (heat) and of hydroxynitriles from aldehydes and ketones with HCN/KCN; hydrolysis of nitriles with dilute acid or with dilute alkali followed by acidification to carboxylic acids; reduction of nitriles to primary amines; use of nitriles to add one carbon atom to a chain in synthesis.

concepts.name: Phenylamine, diazonium salts and azo dyes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Preparation of phenylamine by nitration of benzene and reduction of nitrobenzene with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid followed by NaOH(aq); reaction of phenylamine with bromine water (2,4,6-tribromophenylamine); diazotisation with nitrous acid (NaNO₂ and dilute HCl below 10 °C) and why the temperature is kept low; hydrolysis of the diazonium salt on warming to give phenol; coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol in alkali to form an azo compound; the azo group, azo compounds as dyes (extended delocalisation and colour) and other azo dyes made by similar routes (ZIMSEC: synthesising a dyestuff).

concepts.name: Amides
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Primary, secondary and tertiary amides and their naming (up to six plus six carbons); production from ammonia or a primary amine and an acyl chloride at room temperature; hydrolysis by aqueous acid (carboxylic acid and ammonium salt) or aqueous alkali (carboxylate and ammonia or amine) and deducing the products; reduction of the C=O group of amides with LiAlH₄ to amines; why amides are much weaker bases than amines (delocalisation of the nitrogen lone pair over the C=O group). The peptide bond is achem.amines.amino-acids.

concepts.name: Amino acids, peptides and proteins
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Structure of 2-amino acids and the zwitterion; acid-base properties and the isoelectric point; forms of an amino acid at low, isoelectric and high pH; titration curves of amino acids (ZIMSEC detail); formation of peptide (amide) bonds to give dipeptides and tripeptides and the number of possible sequences; hydrolysis of proteins and peptides (acid, alkali, enzymes) and identifying the products; electrophoresis of mixtures of amino acids and dipeptides at different pH values: direction and relative distance moved from charge and size (assembling the apparatus is not tested). Genetic fingerprinting is achem.analysis.electrophoresis.

concepts.name: Addition polymerisation
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Addition polymerisation of alkenes as exemplified by poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene), PVC (and poly(propene)); deducing the repeat unit from a monomer and the monomer from a section of polymer (written as text formulae); characteristics of addition polymers (saturated backbone, no by-product); low- and high-density poly(ethene) in outline; why poly(alkene)s are difficult to dispose of (non-biodegradable; harmful combustion products such as HCl from PVC).

concepts.name: Condensation polymerisation: polyesters and polyamides
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Formation of polyesters from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid or dioyl chloride, and from a hydroxycarboxylic acid (for example poly(lactic acid)); formation of polyamides from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid or dioyl chloride (nylon-6,6), from an aminocarboxylic acid, and from amino acids (proteins); the small molecule eliminated; deducing repeat units from monomers and monomers from a polymer section; predicting the type of polymerisation for a given monomer or pair of monomers and from a section of polymer; hydrogen bonding between polyamide chains (Kevlar in outline).

concepts.name: Uses of polymers and degradable polymers
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Uses of common addition and condensation polymers related to their properties (poly(ethene), PVC, poly(propene), PTFE, nylon, polyesters such as PET in bottles and clothing, Kevlar); chemical inertness of poly(alkene)s and why they persist in the environment; photodegradable polymers; biodegradability of polyesters and polyamides by acidic and alkaline hydrolysis; disposal options (landfill, incineration, recycling) and plastic litter, presented with balanced, factual points; ZIMSEC suggested site visits in general terms.

concepts.name: Infrared spectroscopy
concepts.description: Cambridge only (AS Level). Absorption of infrared radiation by vibrating bonds; wavenumber (cm⁻¹); using characteristic absorption ranges from the data booklet (O–H in alcohols and in acids, N–H, C–H, C=O, C≡N, C=C, C–O) to identify functional groups in a simple molecule from a described spectrum or a table of peaks; the fingerprint region in outline; following an oxidation (alcohol to aldehyde or acid) by IR; greenhouse gases absorb IR in outline. Cambridge only (AS Level).

concepts.name: Mass spectrometry
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Interpreting mass spectra (given as tables of m/e and relative abundance) in terms of isotopic abundances and molecular fragments; calculating relative atomic mass from a mass spectrum; the molecular ion peak and molecular mass of an organic compound; identifying simple fragment ions (CH₃⁺ 15, C₂H₅⁺ 29, CH₃CO⁺ 43 and others) and suggesting a structure; the number of carbon atoms from the [M+1]⁺ peak, n = 100 × abundance(M+1)/(1.1 × abundance(M)); chlorine and bromine atoms from [M+2]⁺ peaks (3:1 and 1:1 patterns, and molecules with two halogen atoms); the working of the mass spectrometer is not required.

concepts.name: Paper, thin-layer and column chromatography
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Principles of chromatography: stationary phase (cellulose or water in paper; silica or aluminium oxide on a support in TLC and columns), mobile phase (polar or non-polar solvents), adsorption and partition; baseline, solvent front and Rf values; interpreting chromatograms and Rf values (identification by comparison with standards, purity, two-way chromatography in outline, locating agents such as ninhydrin or ultraviolet light); explaining different Rf values from interactions with the stationary phase and solubility in the mobile phase; column chromatography for separation; ion-exchange chromatography in outline (ZIMSEC detail); industrial and medical applications (drug testing, food colourings, amino acids) in general terms.

concepts.name: Gas-liquid chromatography and HPLC
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Gas-liquid chromatography: stationary phase a high-boiling non-polar liquid on a solid support, mobile phase an unreactive carrier gas; retention time and what affects it (boiling point, interaction with the stationary phase, temperature, column length); interpreting gas chromatograms and calculating the percentage composition of a mixture from relative peak areas; high-performance liquid chromatography in outline (ZIMSEC detail); GC-MS and applications such as testing for drugs or contaminants in general terms.

concepts.name: Carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Principles in outline (nuclei in a magnetic field; chemical shift δ in ppm relative to TMS); different carbon environments and the number of peaks predicted for a given molecule (symmetry); using chemical shift ranges from the data booklet (described tables) to deduce the types of carbon present and possible structures; distinguishing isomers by their 13C spectra. Cambridge A Level only.

concepts.name: Proton (1H) NMR spectroscopy
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Chemical shift and proton environments using data-booklet ranges; relative numbers of protons from relative peak areas (integration); splitting by protons on the adjacent carbon atom and the n + 1 rule (singlet, doublet, triplet, quartet, multiplet); deducing structures from described spectra (tables of δ, relative area and splitting) and predicting spectra for given molecules; tetramethylsilane (TMS) as the reference standard; deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃; identifying O–H and N–H protons by exchange with D₂O. Cambridge A Level only.

concepts.name: Electrophoresis and genetic fingerprinting
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Principle of electrophoresis (charged species move in an electric field through a gel or paper buffered at a chosen pH; speed depends on charge and size) and the effect of pH on the charge of amino acids and proteins; hydrolysis of proteins and separation and detection of the products (stains such as ninhydrin) by electrophoresis; outline of the analysis of genes and genetic (DNA) fingerprinting: extraction of DNA, restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis of fragments, probes and the comparison of band patterns, with uses in forensic and paternity work, presented factually. ZIMSEC only (Cambridge electrophoresis of amino acids is in achem.amines.amino-acids).

concepts.name: Air pollution, its control and power generation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Main industrial causes of air pollution (sulfur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, particulates, carbon monoxide); controlling sulfur dioxide emissions: flue-gas desulfurisation, alkaline scrubbing and limestone-based fluidised beds, with equations; lean-burn engines and catalytic converters for petrol cars; environmental considerations in generating power from fossil fuels (coal-fired stations such as those in Zimbabwe in general terms, carbon dioxide and climate change) and from nuclear energy; other potential power sources (hydroelectric, solar, wind, biogas, biofuels) compared; hazards of radon and other emissions from uranium-bearing rocks and of nuclear accidents, stated factually. ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Waste management, water pollution and heavy metals
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Ion exchange in the treatment of industrial waste water; disposal of solid waste by landfill (leachate, methane) and incineration (importance of temperature control, possible release of dioxins); recycling; advantages and disadvantages of dumping waste at sea and in rivers, including sewage (oxygen demand, eutrophication) and oil spills; problems of heavy metals such as lead, mercury (for example from small-scale gold processing, in general terms) and chromium in the environment; disposal of radioactive waste and mine waste (acid mine drainage). ZIMSEC only; no invented statistics.

concepts.name: Nanochemistry: properties and applications of nanomaterials
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Nanoscale (1-100 nm), nanoscience and nanotechnology; why nanoparticles behave differently from bulk material (very large surface area to volume ratio, size-dependent properties); examples: fullerenes, carbon nanotubes, graphene, silver and titanium dioxide nanoparticles; potential applications in medicine (drug delivery), water purification, environmental pollution control and remediation, catalysis, sunscreens and electronics; possible risks (toxicity, unknown long-term effects, entry into cells, environmental release) and the need for regulation, presented in a balanced way. ZIMSEC only.

concepts.name: Quantitative practical work: titrations, measurements and uncertainty
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Practical technique for quantitative work: burette and pipette use, rough and accurate titrations, concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³), burette readings to 0.05 cm³, weighings to 0.01 g, temperatures to 0.5 °C or 0.1 °C as the thermometer allows; standard solutions and weighing by difference; gravimetric (heating to constant mass), thermometric, gas-volume and rate (clock) experiments; recording results in tables with headings and units; significant figures in calculated values (the same as or one more than the least precise data); maximum uncertainty (half the smallest division, doubled for a difference) and percentage error; systematic and random errors; graphs (axes, scales, best-fit lines, gradients and intercepts, extrapolation). Analysis of given data in planning questions is achem.skills.planning-evaluation.

concepts.name: Qualitative analysis: tests for ions, gases and functional groups
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Reactions of the cations NH₄⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺, Cr³⁺, Mn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺ and Pb²⁺ with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia (Pb²⁺ and Mn²⁺ are in the ZIMSEC list); tests for the anions CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻, NO₂⁻, SO₄²⁻, SO₃²⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ and CrO₄²⁻; tests for the gases NH₃, CO₂, Cl₂, H₂, O₂ and SO₂; organic tests (bromine water, Fehling's, Tollens', 2,4-DNPH, alkaline iodine, acidified manganate(VII) or dichromate(VI), sodium carbonate, neutral iron(III) chloride for phenols in outline); safe technique, recording observations precisely and writing deductions linked to each observation; working through an unknown. Use the qualitative-analysis notes printed in the syllabuses as the reference.

concepts.name: Planning, analysis and evaluation of experiments
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Planning: defining the problem, prediction or hypothesis linking the independent and dependent variables, variables to control, apparatus and quantities (volumes, concentrations, masses), a step-by-step method with standard laboratory practice (standard solutions, weighing by difference, concordant titres, heating to constant mass, more readings near an inflexion), safety precautions and risk assessment, results tables and proposed graphs; analysis: calculations from raw data, choosing what to plot, plotting y against x to find m and c in y = mx + c (for example log(rate) against log(concentration) for order, ln k against 1/T in outline only when the equation is given), percentage error; conclusions and evaluation: anomalies, replication, range, control of variables, weaknesses and improvements, validity and confidence. Contexts may lie outside the syllabus.
